placeholders.name: PASTE NOTES
placeholders.what: This is where you paste your raw, unpolished notes from the property walkthrough — bullet points, fragments, and abbreviations are fine, don't clean them up first. Pull them from wherever you actually jotted them: a phone notes app, a paper pad, or a voice memo you typed up afterward. A good set of notes lists concrete facts (room counts, specific upgrades with rough dates, condition issues, price); a weak set just says things like "nice house, good condition" that give Claude nothing specific to work with.
examples: 142 Birchwood Court. 4 bed 2.5 bath single family, built 1998. Roof replaced 2021. New furnace last winter. Hardwood floors in living/dining, carpet in bedrooms. Fenced backyard, deck needs staining. 2-car attached garage. Seller mentioned a school bus stop at the corner (not verified). Asking $610,000.

89 Redwood Terrace #12. Studio apartment, 1 bath, 3rd floor walkup, no elevator. Building built 1975. Recently repainted. Radiator heat, no AC. Monthly fee $240 covers heat and water. Close to the number 12 bus line. Listing price $189,000.

556 Maple Hollow Drive. 3 bed 2 bath ranch. Kitchen original, dated but functional, no major issues noted. New water heater installed 2023. Detached 1-car garage currently used as a workshop. Large corner lot, no fence. Seller relocating for work, open to flexible closing date. No price set yet, waiting on comps.

variations.label: Starting from a voice-memo transcript
variations.whenToUse: Use this when your notes are a messy, run-on paragraph dictated between showings rather than clean bullets — the AI needs an extra step to pull out discrete facts before it can write from them.
variations.prompt:
You are helping me write a real estate listing description from a voice memo I dictated during a walkthrough.

Step 1: Read the transcript below and pull out a clean bullet list of individual, concrete facts (rooms, condition, upgrades, price, anything the seller said). Don't add anything not actually said.

Step 2: STRICT RULE — using only that bullet list, write a 150-200 word MLS-style listing description in a warm, professional tone, plus a one-sentence headline. If a fact that would normally appear in a listing is missing, list it under "Missing facts to confirm" instead of guessing.

Transcript:
[PASTE VOICE MEMO TRANSCRIPT]

Audience: buyers browsing listing sites. Do not mention price unless the transcript states it.

variations.label: Luxury / high-end listing version
variations.whenToUse: Use for listings priced well above your market's typical range, where buyers expect more evocative, detailed copy and a longer word count is standard practice.
variations.prompt:
You are helping me write a luxury real estate listing description.

STRICT RULE: Use only the facts in the notes below. Do not invent finishes, brands, views, acreage, or amenities not explicitly stated — no guessing at "designer" fixtures or square footage. If a fact that would normally appear in a luxury listing is missing, list it under "Missing facts to confirm."

My raw notes:
[PASTE NOTES]

Write:
1. A 250-300 word listing description with a more sensory, evocative tone appropriate for a luxury buyer — still grounded entirely in stated facts, no hype adjectives without something concrete behind them.
2. A one-sentence headline.
3. A "Missing facts to confirm" list.

Audience: high-net-worth buyers browsing premium listing sites.

variations.label: Starting from a seller's disclosure sheet, not walkthrough notes
variations.whenToUse: Use when you're drafting an early listing description before your own showing, working only from the seller's completed property disclosure form.
variations.prompt:
You are helping me write a real estate listing description from a seller's property disclosure form, before I've done my own walkthrough.

STRICT RULE: Use only facts explicitly stated in the disclosure text below. Do not invent condition, upgrades, or features it doesn't mention, and do not include anything the disclosure states as a problem or defect unless I ask you to phrase it neutrally for marketing — flag those separately instead.

Disclosure form text:
[PASTE DISCLOSURE FORM TEXT]

Write:
1. A 150-200 word draft listing description, clearly marked as a DRAFT pending my own walkthrough.
2. A "Missing facts to confirm" list, including anything I should verify in person before publishing.
3. A separate "Disclosed issues to handle carefully" list of anything the disclosure flagged that should not appear in marketing copy.

followUps.label: Check it didn't invent anything
followUps.prompt: Go back through the draft you just wrote and compare it sentence by sentence against my original notes. List any word, number, or claim in the draft that isn't directly traceable to something I gave you, even if it seems minor (like changing "updated" to "renovated"). If you find none, say so explicitly.

followUps.label: Too long for my MLS field? Cut it down
followUps.prompt: My MLS system has a 750-character limit including spaces. Shorten the description to fit while keeping every fact — cut phrasing and filler first, never a fact, and tell me the final character count.

followUps.label: Make the headline punchier
followUps.prompt: Give me 5 alternative one-sentence headlines for this listing, each highlighting a different verified detail from my notes, none over 65 characters.

followUps.label: Fair-housing check
followUps.prompt: Reread the description and flag any word or phrase that could be read as describing the type of buyer or resident the home would suit, rather than the property itself, even indirectly.

re-b1-listing-from-notes.walkthrough:
Sofia Marlowe, an agent at Harborview Realty, had just wrapped a walkthrough of 142 Birchwood Court and needed a listing description before her next showing in forty minutes. During the walkthrough she had typed rough notes into her phone: four bedrooms, roof replaced in 2021, a new furnace, hardwood floors in the main living areas, a fenced backyard with a deck that needed staining, a two-car garage, and an asking price of $610,000. The seller had also mentioned a school bus stop at the corner, but Sofia hadn't verified that herself.

She opened Claude on her phone, pasted the guardrail prompt from this lesson, and dropped her notes in place of [PASTE NOTES]. She asked for the standard MLS-style description under 200 words, a headline, and a missing-facts list.

Claude's draft opened with a headline built around the fenced backyard and hardwood floors, wrote a 180-word description covering the roof, furnace, floors, garage, and yard, and correctly left out the school bus comment since Sofia hadn't confirmed it. Under "Missing facts to confirm," it flagged square footage and year built as absent from her notes — both true gaps.

Before publishing, Sofia sent the follow-up asking Claude to check the draft against her notes line by line. Claude confirmed everything traced back cleanly, but flagged that it had written "updated furnace" where her notes said "new furnace" — a small but real distinction, so she corrected it.

She pulled the square footage from the county property record in two minutes, added it herself, and had a publish-ready listing eleven minutes after she'd started — well before her next appointment.

placeholders.name: PASTE CURRENT DESCRIPTION
placeholders.what: This is the existing listing text, copied exactly as it's published right now, flaws and clichés included. Find it on your MLS listing page, Zillow, or wherever you originally posted it. Paste the full text, not a summary of it — Claude needs the actual wording to know what it's allowed to keep, cut, or rephrase.
examples: Charming home in a great location! 3 bedrooms, 2 baths. Freshly painted. Won't last long!
Spacious 1-bedroom condo close to everything. Great building. Priced to sell fast!
This lovely ranch has so much to offer. Updated kitchen. Big yard. A must-see!

placeholders.name: TARGET WORD COUNT
placeholders.what: The word count you want the rewrite to land near — usually whatever fits your MLS description field or matches your platform's typical length. Give a specific number, not a vague range, so Claude has something concrete to hit.
examples: 150 words (fits our MLS description field with room to spare)
200 words (standard length for our brokerage's Zillow feed)
90 words (short blurb for a postcard mailer)

placeholders.name: e.g., warm and professional / upbeat and modern
placeholders.what: Replace this entire bracket with the tone that fits your brokerage's voice and the property type — don't leave the "e.g." in your actual message. Pick from the menu below or describe your own in a few words.
examples: Warm and professional — for most resale listings
Upbeat and modern — for condos and starter homes aimed at first-time buyers
Quietly upscale and understated — for luxury listings where restraint reads as confidence

variations.label: Rewriting for a different platform than MLS
variations.whenToUse: Use when you need a shorter, more casual version for Zillow's "agent remarks," Facebook Marketplace, or a postcard, rather than your formal MLS field.
variations.prompt:
Here is my current listing description:
[PASTE CURRENT DESCRIPTION]

Rewrite it for [PLATFORM, e.g. Zillow public remarks / Facebook Marketplace / a printed postcard] while following these rules:
- Do not add any fact, feature, upgrade, or claim that is not already stated in the text above.
- Match the shorter, more casual register typical of that platform.
- Keep length to roughly [TARGET WORD COUNT] words.

After the rewrite, add a "Facts changed or added" section listing anywhere your wording could be read as adding a new fact. If there are none, say "None."

variations.label: Bulk rewrite for several stale listings at once
variations.whenToUse: Use on a slow Friday when you want to refresh your 3-5 oldest active listings in one pass instead of one at a time.
variations.prompt:
I'm going to give you several current listing descriptions. Rewrite each one separately using these rules for every one:
- Do not add any fact, feature, upgrade, or claim not already stated in that listing's text.
- Tighten sentences and replace generic phrases with more specific ones describing the SAME facts.
- Keep each rewrite to roughly [TARGET WORD COUNT] words.

After each rewrite, add a "Facts changed or added" note for that listing.

Listing 1:
[PASTE CURRENT DESCRIPTION]

Listing 2:
[PASTE CURRENT DESCRIPTION]

Listing 3:
[PASTE CURRENT DESCRIPTION]

variations.label: Repositioning after a price reduction
variations.whenToUse: Use when the description needs to reflect renewed value after a price cut, without resorting to urgency language or changing any fact.
variations.prompt:
Here is my current listing description:
[PASTE CURRENT DESCRIPTION]

The price on this listing was recently reduced. Rewrite the description to reframe the property's value for a buyer re-evaluating it, following these rules:
- Do not add any fact, feature, upgrade, or claim not already stated above.
- Do not use urgency or scarcity language ("won't last," "act now," "priced to sell").
- Emphasize the SAME stated facts in a way that reads as genuine value, not desperation.
- Keep length to roughly [TARGET WORD COUNT] words. Tone: [e.g., warm and professional / upbeat and modern].

After the rewrite, add a "Facts changed or added" section.

followUps.label: Double-check the fact-diff more strictly
followUps.prompt: Re-read your rewrite one more time, sentence by sentence, and look specifically for words that intensify a claim beyond what the original said — like "updated" becoming "fully renovated" or "nice" becoming "stunning." List every instance, even ones you already flagged.

followUps.label: Give me headline options within my character limit
followUps.prompt: Give me 3 headline options for this listing, each under 60 characters so it fits my MLS headline field, each highlighting a different fact from the original description.

followUps.label: Still sounds generic — make it more specific
followUps.prompt: This still reads a bit generic. Using only the facts already in the text, replace any remaining vague phrase (like "great location" or "lots of natural light") with more specific, sensory language that describes that exact same fact.

followUps.label: Match my brokerage's voice
followUps.prompt: Here's a sample of how our brokerage usually writes listing copy: [PASTE SAMPLE COPY]. Rewrite the draft again to match that voice and sentence rhythm, without changing any fact.

re-b2-improve-listing-description.walkthrough:
Jordan Reyes had a studio listing at 89 Redwood Terrace #12 that had been sitting active for five weeks with almost no showings. The description was the generic kind every agent writes when they're rushed: "Spacious 1-bedroom condo close to everything. Great building. Priced to sell fast!" It didn't mention anything a buyer could picture, and Jordan suspected that was part of why it wasn't getting traffic.

Jordan opened Claude, pasted the rewrite prompt, dropped the existing description in for [PASTE CURRENT DESCRIPTION], set the target word count to 150, and chose "upbeat and modern" as the tone since the building attracted younger first-time buyers.

Claude's rewrite kept every original fact but replaced "great building" with a description of the recent repaint and the radiator heat included in the monthly fee, and dropped "priced to sell fast" entirely since it read as pressure rather than information. The "Facts changed or added" section came back with one flag: the draft had implied the unit was "move-in ready," a phrase not in the original text.

Jordan sent the follow-up asking Claude to re-check for any word that intensified a claim beyond the original. Claude caught the same "move-in ready" phrase again and suggested removing it, since nothing in the original description supported it. Jordan cut the line.

With the fact-diff clean, Jordan asked for three headline options under 60 characters, picked one referencing the walkup building's recent repaint, and swapped it into the live MLS listing. The whole rewrite, including both review passes, took about nine minutes — faster than Jordan expected for a listing that had felt stuck for over a month.

placeholders.name: BUYER NAME
placeholders.what: The buyer's first name, or both names if you showed the property to a couple or group. Use whatever they introduced themselves as — don't guess at a formal name if they went by a nickname during the showing.
examples: Marcus and Priya Chen
Jordan T.
the Alvarez family

placeholders.name: ADDRESS / SHORT DESCRIPTION
placeholders.what: The property you showed them, either as the full address or a short description they'd recognize if they saw multiple homes that day. Being specific here helps Claude write an email that clearly refers to the right property, not a generic "the home we saw."
examples: 27 Aspen Grove Lane, Unit 4B
142 Birchwood Court (the 4-bed colonial on the cul-de-sac)
89 Redwood Terrace #12 (the studio walkup)

placeholders.name: NOTES
placeholders.what: This bracket is used twice: once for what the buyer liked, once for what concerned them or what they asked about. In both spots, write 1-3 short phrases capturing their actual reactions and questions, ideally close to their own words — this is what makes the email feel personal instead of like a form letter. A weak note just says "seemed interested"; a good one captures a specific reaction or question.
examples: Loved the open kitchen layout and the natural light in the living room; asked twice about the monthly fee
Thought the primary bedroom felt small for the price; liked the finished basement a lot
Really responded to the backyard and how quiet the cul-de-sac was; asked about the age of the roof

placeholders.name: e.g., invite them to a second showing this weekend / send similar listings / find out their decision timeline
placeholders.what: Pick the single most useful next step for this specific buyer, based on how the showing went. Replace the whole bracket with your actual goal — don't leave more than one goal in, since the prompt is built to produce one clear ask, not several competing ones.
examples: Invite them back for a second showing this Saturday afternoon
Send them 2-3 similar listings that just hit the market this week
Find out their financing timeline and whether they're pre-approved yet

variations.label: Re-engaging a buyer who went quiet
variations.whenToUse: Use when this is your second or third attempt to reach a buyer who hasn't responded to earlier follow-ups, and you want to re-open the door without sounding needy or repetitive.
variations.prompt:
Write a re-engagement email to a buyer who hasn't responded to my last two follow-ups after a showing.

Buyer: [BUYER NAME]
Property shown: [ADDRESS / SHORT DESCRIPTION]
What they liked / asked about originally: [NOTES]
What's changed since then, if anything (price drop, new comparable listing, etc.): [UPDATE OR "nothing new"]

Rules:
- Acknowledge lightly that you haven't heard back, without guilt-tripping.
- Give them a genuine reason to re-engage (the update above, or a specific question), not just "just checking in."
- Keep it under 100 words.
- End with a low-friction next step they can ignore easily if they've moved on — a single yes/no question works well.

Do not invent details about the property or buyer beyond what I've given you.

variations.label: Short text-message version
variations.whenToUse: Use right after a showing when you want to send something within minutes, before you have time to write a full email.
variations.prompt:
Write a text message to a buyer after a home showing, under 320 characters.

Buyer: [BUYER NAME]
Property shown: [ADDRESS / SHORT DESCRIPTION]
What they liked: [NOTES]
My goal: [e.g., invite them to a second showing this weekend / send similar listings / find out their decision timeline]

Rules:
- Reference one specific detail from what they liked.
- Casual but professional tone, no pressure language.
- End with one simple question.

Do not invent any detail I haven't given you.

variations.label: Following up with several buyers from one open house
variations.whenToUse: Use after an open house where you collected notes on multiple visitors and need individualized emails without writing each one from scratch.
variations.prompt:
I showed several buyers through an open house today. Write a separate, individually personalized follow-up email for each one below, following these rules for every email:
- Reference at least one specific detail from what that buyer liked or asked.
- Keep each under 150 words, warm tone, no pressure language.
- End each with one clear next step suited to that buyer.
- Do not invent details about the property or any buyer beyond what I've given you.

Property shown: [ADDRESS / SHORT DESCRIPTION]

Buyer 1: [BUYER NAME] — liked/asked: [NOTES] — goal: [GOAL]
Buyer 2: [BUYER NAME] — liked/asked: [NOTES] — goal: [GOAL]
Buyer 3: [BUYER NAME] — liked/asked: [NOTES] — goal: [GOAL]

followUps.label: Subject line feels generic
followUps.prompt: Give me 3 alternative subject lines under 8 words, each referencing a specific detail from what the buyer liked, not a generic phrase like "Following up."

followUps.label: Too salesy — dial it back
followUps.prompt: This reads a bit too eager. Rewrite it so it feels more like a helpful note from someone who was genuinely glad to show them the home, with less emphasis on pushing toward a decision.

followUps.label: Shorten it for a text message
followUps.prompt: Condense this into a text message under 320 characters, keeping the one specific detail and the single call to action, but dropping the greeting and sign-off formality.

followUps.label: Double-check no invented details
followUps.prompt: Reread the email and confirm every detail about the property or the buyer's reaction came directly from what I gave you. Flag anything you added or guessed at, even something small.

re-b3-buyer-followup-emails.walkthrough:
Sofia Marlowe showed 27 Aspen Grove Lane, Unit 4B to Marcus and Priya Chen on a Tuesday evening. Walking back to her car afterward, she typed three lines into her phone: they loved the balcony and the afternoon light in the living room, they asked twice whether the monthly HOA fee included water, and Priya mentioned being a little concerned there was no dedicated storage unit in the building.

Back at her desk twenty minutes later, Sofia opened Claude and pasted the follow-up email prompt. She filled in "Marcus and Priya Chen" for the buyer name, the unit address, her three lines of notes split across the "liked" and "concerned" fields, and set her goal as inviting them back for a second showing that Saturday.

Claude's draft opened by naming the balcony and the afternoon light specifically, noted that Sofia would confirm the exact HOA fee breakdown for them, acknowledged the storage question honestly rather than glossing over it, and closed with a single question asking if Saturday afternoon worked for a second look. The subject line it suggested was "Still thinking about that balcony?" — a little generic for Sofia's taste.

She sent the follow-up asking for three sharper subject line options, each referencing something specific from the showing. Claude returned three, and Sofia picked one that mentioned the afternoon light directly.

Before sending, she skimmed the email once more against her original three lines and confirmed nothing had been added that she hadn't actually told Claude. The whole process, from typing her notes in the parking lot to sending the email, took under fifteen minutes — and Priya replied within the hour confirming Saturday.

placeholders.name: ADDRESS
placeholders.what: The property address for the listing this update covers. Use the same address format your seller would recognize from your other communications with them.
examples: 27 Aspen Grove Lane, Unit 4B
142 Birchwood Court
556 Maple Hollow Drive

placeholders.name: NUMBER
placeholders.what: The actual count of showings held this week, pulled from your showing-service app or your own calendar — not an estimate. If there were zero, write 0 rather than skipping the field.

placeholders.name: NUMBER OR "not tracked"
placeholders.what: The number of online views from Zillow, your MLS portal, or wherever you track them this week. If your brokerage doesn't give you this data, write "not tracked" honestly rather than guessing at a number.
examples: 142 views on Zillow this week, up from 98 last week
not tracked
58 portal views

placeholders.name: PASTE RAW FEEDBACK NOTES, e.g. "liked the kitchen, thought price was high, one buyer said yard was small"
placeholders.what: Whatever feedback you actually collected from showing agents or buyers this week, in your own shorthand — don't smooth it over before pasting it in. Include both positive and negative comments exactly as given; the prompt is built to preserve negative feedback honestly, so holding it back here defeats the point.
examples: Two buyers liked the open layout; one said the price felt high given there's no dedicated parking spot; one buyer's agent said their client is deciding between this unit and a listing two blocks over
Only one showing this week, agent said client loved the kitchen but was put off by the building's exterior needing paint
Three showings, consistent comment that the primary bathroom feels dated; one buyer asked if the seller would consider a credit toward updating it

placeholders.name: NONE / DETAILS
placeholders.what: Whether there's any offer or serious buyer interest to report this week. If there's genuinely nothing, write "None" plainly rather than implying vague interest exists — this is the field where sellers most need honesty over optimism.
examples: None
One buyer emailed asking about seller flexibility on closing date — no formal offer yet
Verbal offer at $395,000, contingent on inspection; buyer's agent says they'll submit in writing Monday

placeholders.name: OPTIONAL
placeholders.what: Use this only if you want the update to also open a strategy conversation, like a price adjustment or staging change, based on a pattern you're seeing in the feedback. Leave it out or write "none this week" if you're not ready to raise anything yet.
examples: I want to gently raise whether we should consider a $10,000 price adjustment given the repeated price comments
None this week
I want to suggest professional staging photos given repeated comments about the rooms feeling dark

variations.label: Text-only quick update
variations.whenToUse: Use for sellers who've told you they prefer texting over email, or when you only have a couple of minutes between showings.
variations.prompt:
Write a text-message-only seller update summarizing this week's activity, under 400 characters.

Property: [ADDRESS]
Showings this week: [NUMBER]
Buyer feedback: [PASTE RAW FEEDBACK NOTES]
Offers or serious interest: [NONE / DETAILS]

Rules:
- Report the facts honestly, including negative feedback — do not soften or omit it.
- Do not speculate about buyer intentions beyond what's stated.
- Calm, professional tone, reassuring without being falsely upbeat.
- If there's a pattern across multiple pieces of feedback, mention it plainly.

variations.label: Multi-week trend update
variations.whenToUse: Use once a listing has been active for a month or more and the seller needs to see the trend across weeks, not just this week in isolation.
variations.prompt:
Write a seller update that compares this week's activity to the prior weeks on this listing.

Property: [ADDRESS]
This week — showings: [NUMBER], views: [NUMBER OR "not tracked"], feedback: [PASTE RAW FEEDBACK NOTES], offers: [NONE / DETAILS]
Prior weeks' totals for comparison: [PASTE PRIOR WEEKS' NUMBERS, e.g. "Week 1: 6 showings, Week 2: 4 showings, Week 3: 2 showings"]

Rules:
- Report all figures exactly as given, including if the trend is declining — do not soften a downward trend.
- Point out the trend plainly (increasing, flat, or declining interest) using only the numbers provided.
- Tone: calm, honest, professional.
- Produce one email version, 150-200 words, with a simple week-by-week comparison.

variations.label: A quiet week with no showings
variations.whenToUse: Use for the hardest version of this update — a week with zero activity — where honesty and reassurance both matter most.
variations.prompt:
Write a seller update for a week with no showings on their listing.

Property: [ADDRESS]
Showings this week: 0
Online views: [NUMBER OR "not tracked"]
Any inquiries that didn't convert to a showing: [DETAILS OR "none"]
What I plan to do about it: [e.g., "reduce price by $8,000" / "refresh photos" / "nothing yet, monitoring"]

Rules:
- State plainly that there were no showings — do not disguise this with vague positive language.
- If I've given you a planned action, present it clearly as a proactive next step, not an apology.
- If I haven't given you a planned action, do not invent one — instead suggest I discuss options with the seller.
- Tone: calm and professional, not falsely upbeat.
- Produce a short text version and a 100-150 word email version.

followUps.label: Make sure nothing was softened
followUps.prompt: Reread the update you just wrote and compare it against my raw feedback notes. Point out any place where negative feedback might read as more neutral or positive than what I actually gave you.

followUps.label: Draft the price conversation as a separate message
followUps.prompt: Based on the repeated feedback pattern, draft a separate, standalone message opening a conversation with the seller about a possible price adjustment or staging change. Keep it separate from the weekly update, honest about why I'm raising it now, and don't recommend a specific new price — that's my call to make with them.

followUps.label: Shorten the email version
followUps.prompt: Cut the email version down to under 120 words without losing any of the reported facts or the honest tone — trim explanation, not content.

followUps.label: Add a comparison to last week
followUps.prompt: Here are last week's numbers: [PASTE LAST WEEK'S SHOWINGS/VIEWS/FEEDBACK]. Add a short comparison to this week's update so the seller can see whether interest is picking up or slowing down.

re-b4-seller-update-messages.walkthrough:
The Ortega family had their condo at 27 Aspen Grove Lane, Unit 4B on the market for three weeks, and Sofia Marlowe made it a habit to send them a Friday update no matter how the week had gone. This week: three showings, feedback that two buyers liked the open layout, one buyer's agent mentioned their client felt the price was high given the lack of a dedicated parking spot, and no offers.

Sofia opened Claude and pasted the seller update prompt, filling in the address, three showings, her rough feedback notes exactly as she'd written them, "None" for offers, and left the optional price-conversation field blank since she wasn't ready to raise that yet.

Claude's draft reported the three showings and the layout compliments honestly, then stated plainly that the price-versus-parking comment had come up, without softening it into something vaguer like "buyers had some thoughts on pricing." It produced both a short text version and a slightly longer email, and it noted that this was the second week in a row a similar parking comment had surfaced — a pattern Sofia hadn't consciously tracked herself.

That pattern note made Sofia decide to raise the topic with the Ortegas. She sent the follow-up asking Claude to draft a separate message opening a price or staging conversation, based on the repeated feedback, without suggesting a specific new number.

Sofia sent the honest weekly update by text that afternoon, then scheduled a call with the Ortegas for Monday using the separate conversation-starter draft as her outline. The whole task took about seven minutes, and the honesty paid off — the Ortegas thanked her for flagging the pattern instead of letting it drag on.

placeholders.name: inspection report / seller disclosure / HOA document
placeholders.what: Name which type of document you're summarizing so Claude knows what structure and vocabulary to expect. Pick the one that actually matches what you're uploading — an inspection report and an HOA covenant document need very different handling.
examples: inspection report
seller disclosure
HOA covenant document

placeholders.name: PASTE OR UPLOAD DOCUMENT
placeholders.what: The actual document text (or the uploaded file itself). If pasting text, include the full document, not just the parts that seem important — a partial paste produces a summary that looks complete but is missing whatever you left out. If uploading, say so in your message and skip the paste.
examples: Roof: architectural shingles, installed approx. 2014, no active leaks observed, minor granule loss noted in northeast corner. Electrical: panel is a Federal Pacific Electric (FPE) panel, flagged for evaluation by a licensed electrician due to known safety recall history on this panel brand. Plumbing: galvanized supply lines in upstairs bathroom showing surface corrosion; recommend evaluation by a licensed plumber. HVAC: furnace original to 1998 construction, functional at time of inspection, nearing typical end of service life.

Seller discloses: water intrusion in basement occurred in 2019 following heavy rain, repaired by contractor with new sump pump installed same year, no recurrence reported since. Seller is not aware of any pending special assessments. Seller discloses one bathroom renovation completed without a permit in 2016.

HOA document excerpt: Monthly assessment is $310, covering water, trash, and exterior building maintenance. Rentals are permitted with a minimum 6-month lease term and require board approval. Two pets per unit permitted, combined weight limit 80 lbs. Reserve fund currently funded at approximately 60% of the reserve study's recommended level.

variations.label: When you only have a scanned or photographed document
variations.whenToUse: Use when the document came through as a phone photo or a scanned PDF rather than clean text, where some words or numbers may be unclear or cut off.
variations.prompt:
I'm uploading a [inspection report / seller disclosure / HOA document] for a property. This came from a scan/photo, so some text may be unclear or partially cut off. Summarize it for my client using only what's in the document.

Rules:
- Use only information you can clearly read in the document. Do not add general knowledge or predict repair costs unless a cost is stated.
- If any section is illegible, cut off, or ambiguous, list it explicitly under a new category: "Could not read clearly — needs the original document."
- Organize the rest into: (1) Major issues / safety items, (2) Moderate issues / maintenance items, (3) Minor / cosmetic notes, (4) Anything unclear that needs a professional to clarify.
- End with this exact disclaimer: "This is a plain-language summary for convenience only. It is not a substitute for reading the full document or for advice from a licensed inspector, attorney, or other qualified professional."

Document:
[PASTE OR UPLOAD DOCUMENT]

variations.label: Internal prep summary, not for the client
variations.whenToUse: Use when you want a denser summary for your own negotiation prep before a client conversation, rather than the client-facing version.
variations.prompt:
I'm uploading/pasting a [inspection report / seller disclosure / HOA document] for a property. This summary is for MY internal prep before I talk to my client, not to send to them directly.

Each came with a likely pushback — for the data-led approach, Claude predicted the buyer's agent might argue the kitchen renovation wasn't worth $20,000, and suggested Sofia have a rough sense of renovation cost ready, without inventing a number itself.

Sofia sent the follow-up asking Claude to roleplay the buyer's agent pushing back hard on the data-led approach. She practiced her response twice out loud, adjusting her phrasing until it felt natural rather than rehearsed.

The prep took about ten minutes. On the actual call that afternoon, the buyer's agent raised almost exactly the objection Claude had predicted, and Sofia's practiced, specific answer kept the conversation moving toward an offer instead of a stall.

re-i4-local-market-research-perplexity.walkthrough:
Sofia Marlowe had a listing presentation coming up for a condo owner in Willow Creek and wanted current, cited market data rather than repeating last quarter's numbers from memory.

She opened the Gemini app and started a Deep Research session instead of a normal chat, then pasted the market-research prompt, filling in "Willow Creek neighborhood" for the area, "the last quarter" for the timeframe, and "condos" for the property type. Gemini showed her a short research plan first — she confirmed it covered price, days on market, and inventory, and let it run.

About ten minutes later, the report came back: median condo sale price in Willow Creek was up 4% over the quarter according to a regional MLS data aggregator dated three weeks earlier, average days on market had dropped from 38 to 26 days per a local real estate board report, and active inventory was down about 15% compared to the prior quarter, citing the same board report. It characterized the segment as leaning toward a seller's market given the combination of falling days-on-market and shrinking inventory, and noted it had to widen slightly to zip-code-level data for the inventory figure since neighborhood-specific numbers weren't published separately.

Sofia clicked through two of the citations herself, confirmed both were legitimate, recently published sources, and sent the follow-up asking Gemini to turn the findings into a client-ready paragraph with the source links kept visible.

She pasted that paragraph directly into her listing presentation deck, noting the date she'd run the research so she'd know to refresh it if the appointment got pushed back more than a couple of weeks. The whole research task took about fifteen minutes, most of it waiting on the report, and having cited figures rather than a verbal claim made the pricing conversation with her client noticeably smoother than past presentations.

Every Friday afternoon, Sofia Marlowe faced the same pile of scattered notes: texts from new leads, a stack of open-house sign-in sheets, and a couple of portal inquiry emails she'd flagged but not organized.
